title: Words you will see
summary: Plain explanations of the computer words used in MendKit and in these guides.

sections.heading: About the computer
steps: Operating system (or "system"): the main software that runs the computer: Windows, macOS on a Mac, or Linux (Ubuntu, Mint, Fedora and others).
Drive (hard drive, SSD, disk): where files are stored even when the power is off. An SSD is the fast modern kind with no moving parts; a hard drive (HDD) spins and is much slower.
Memory (RAM): the short-term workspace the computer uses while it is switched on. More memory lets more programs run at once without slowing down.
Processor (CPU): the chip that does the computer's work. Heavy tests make it hot, which is normal up to a point.
Partition and volume: a drive can be split into sections. Each section that holds files is a volume, shown as a drive letter (C:, D:) on Windows or a name on a Mac.
Firmware, BIOS and UEFI: the small built-in program that starts the computer before Windows or macOS loads. It is where you choose to start from a USB stick.
Driver: a small program that lets the system talk to a piece of hardware such as a printer, graphics card or Wi-Fi card.

sections.heading: About repairs
steps: Administrator (admin): an account allowed to change the whole computer. Most repairs need it. See "Administrator rights and passwords".
Restore point (Windows): a snapshot of Windows' settings and system files taken before a change, so the change can be rolled back. It does not back up your documents or photos.
Backup: a separate copy of your files on another drive or online. The only real protection against losing them.
Recipe: in MendKit, a list of checks and fixes run one after another for one problem, such as "No internet".
Tweak: in MendKit, a single setting change that can always be put back.
Log: the complete record of what a command printed while it ran. Technicians use it to see exactly what happened.
Quarantine: a folder where MendKit moves something it removed instead of deleting it, so it can be put back from the Undo Center.

sections.heading: About files and downloads
steps: ISO file: a single file holding an entire disc, such as a Windows installer or a rescue system. It is copied to a USB stick so a computer can start from it.
Bootable USB stick: a stick a computer can start from instead of its own drive. Needed to repair a computer that will not start.
Installer: the file that adds a program to the computer, usually ending .exe or .msi on Windows, .dmg or .pkg on a Mac.
Portable program: runs straight from its file or folder without being installed.
Command line, Terminal, Command Prompt, PowerShell: a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Some tools only work this way.
Package manager (winget, Homebrew, apt and others): the system's own app store for programs, used by MendKit to install tools safely from their official sources.

sections.heading: About networks
steps: Router: the box from your internet company that makes your Wi-Fi and connects your home to the internet.
IP address: the number the router gives each device on the network, such as 192.168.1.20.
DNS: the internet's phone book that turns names like google.com into addresses. When DNS fails, websites will not load even though the connection is up.
Ethernet: a network cable plugged into the computer, as opposed to Wi-Fi.

title: Administrator rights and passwords
summary: What "administrator" means, how to give MendKit those rights on each system, and what to do with a standard account.

sections.heading: Why it matters
steps: Repairs change system files and settings. Windows, macOS and Linux only let an administrator do that, to stop harmful programs doing it behind your back.
Without administrator rights MendKit still runs, but repair steps that need them are skipped and marked "Skipped, needs administrator".
MendKit never stores your password. On a Mac and Linux it asks the system to prompt you, and the system checks the password, not MendKit.

sections.heading: On Windows

steps.t: Open MendKit. On the Dashboard, click Restart as administrator.
steps.see: Windows dims the screen and asks "Do you want to allow this app to make changes to your device?"

steps.t: Click Yes.
steps.see: MendKit closes and opens again. The badge at the bottom left now says Administrator in green.
steps.tip: If Windows asks for a password instead of showing a Yes button, your account is a standard account. Type the name and password of an administrator on this computer.

steps: To start MendKit as administrator every time, right-click its icon on the desktop or Start menu, choose More, then Run as administrator.

sections.heading: On a Mac

steps.t: Nothing to do in advance. When a step needs administrator rights, MendKit asks once for the password you use to sign in to the Mac.
steps.see: A small box titled with the step's name asks for your password. Type it and click OK. Nothing appears as you type; that is normal.

steps: If the account is not an administrator, macOS asks for an administrator's name and password instead. Find out in System Settings, Users & Groups: it says "Admin" under the account name.
MendKit asks only once for a whole job, so you can leave it running.

sections.heading: On Linux

steps.t: When a step needs it, MendKit asks for your password once through the system's own password window (polkit) or sudo.
steps.see: A password box from the system, not from MendKit.

steps: Your account must be allowed to use sudo. On Ubuntu and Mint the first account created is.

sections.heading: If something goes wrong
steps: Forgotten the Windows password for a Microsoft account: reset it at account.live.com/password/reset from any device.
Forgotten a Mac password: on the password screen click the question mark, or restart in Recovery and use Reset Password.
Typing the password and nothing happens: check Caps Lock, and on a laptop check that the number keys are not acting as a number pad.

title: Opening Terminal and typing a command
summary: How to open the command window on each system, type a command exactly, and read what comes back. Several tools work only this way.

sections.heading: Before you start
steps: You do not need to learn the command line. The guides give each command to copy exactly.
Copy commands from the guide rather than typing them where you can: one wrong space or letter changes the meaning.
Commands that start with sudo change the system and ask for your password.

steps.t: Click Start, type Terminal (on Windows 10, type PowerShell) and click it.
steps.see: A dark window with a line ending in > and a blinking cursor. That line is the prompt.

steps.t: For a command that needs administrator rights, right-click Terminal in the Start menu instead and choose Run as administrator, then click Yes.
steps.see: The window title starts with "Administrator".

sections.heading: Open it on a Mac

steps.t: Press Command and Space together, type Terminal and press Return.
steps.see: A window with a line ending in % or $. Your name and the Mac's name are on that line.

steps: Or open Finder, Applications, Utilities, Terminal.

steps.t: Press Ctrl, Alt and T together. If nothing happens, open the applications menu and type Terminal.
steps.see: A window with a line ending in $.

sections.heading: Type a command and read the result

steps.t: Click inside the window. Paste the command (Ctrl+V on Windows, Command+V on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+V on Linux) or type it exactly.
ex: What it looks like on Windows before you type:
C:\Users\Ann>
After pasting a command and pressing Enter:
C:\Users\Ann> ipconfig
Windows IP Configuration ... IPv4 Address. . . : 192.168.1.20
C:\Users\Ann>   ← the prompt comes back when the command has finished

steps.t: Press Enter (Return on a Mac).
steps.see: The command prints its result, then a new prompt line appears when it has finished.
steps.tip: A command that is still working shows no new prompt. Wait for it.

steps.t: If it asks for a password, type it and press Enter. Nothing appears on screen while you type a password; that is normal.
ex: [sudo] password for ann:   ← type the password here; the cursor does not move
Password:   ← the same on a Mac

steps.t: To stop a command that is running, hold Ctrl and press C.
ex: The command stops and the prompt comes back, for example: ^C then ann@laptop:~$

steps.t: Read the last few lines. Words such as "error", "not found" or "permission denied" mean it did not work.
steps.tip: "command not found" or "is not recognized" means the tool is not installed or the name was mistyped. Install it from MendKit's Tools screen.

steps: To copy the result for a technician, select the text with the mouse and press Ctrl+C (Command+C on a Mac). On Windows Terminal, selecting the text copies it.

title: Starting a computer from a USB stick
summary: How to make a computer start from a rescue or installer USB stick instead of its own drive, with the key to press for each brand.
need: A USB stick prepared with Ventoy or Rufus
The computer plugged into power

sections.heading: Boot menu keys by brand

steps.t: Dell: F12. HP: F9, or Esc then F9. Lenovo laptops: F12 (or the small Novo button with a curved arrow). Lenovo desktops: F12.
ex: Press the key again and again (about twice a second) from the moment you press the power button until a menu appears. Holding it down does not work on most computers.

steps: Acer: F12 (turn on "F12 Boot Menu" in the BIOS first if it does nothing). Asus: F8 or Esc. MSI: F11. Gigabyte: F12. Toshiba/Dynabook: F12. Samsung: F2 or Esc. Microsoft Surface: hold Volume Down while pressing power.
Custom-built PCs: watch the first screen for "Boot Menu" or "BBS" and the key next to it; usually F8, F11 or F12.

sections.heading: On a Windows PC

steps.t: Plug the USB stick in while the computer is off. Then switch it on and tap the boot menu key for the computer's brand.
ex: A boot menu looks like this:
Windows Boot Manager (Samsung SSD 970)
UEFI: SanDisk Ultra 1.00   ← choose the USB stick, with UEFI in front if offered
Network boot (IPv4)

steps.t: Press the power button, then immediately tap the boot menu key for your brand about twice a second.
steps.see: A list titled Boot Menu, Boot Device or Please select boot device, with the drive and the USB stick (often by its maker's name, such as SanDisk or Kingston).
steps.tip: If Windows starts instead, the computer was not fully off. In Windows, hold Shift while you click Restart, then choose Use a device and pick the USB stick.

steps.t: Use the arrow keys to pick the USB stick (if it is listed twice, choose the one starting UEFI) and press Enter.
steps.see: The stick's menu, such as Ventoy's list of ISO files, or the installer starting.

steps: When you have finished, remove the stick and restart. The computer starts from its own drive again.

sections.heading: On a Mac
steps: Apple silicon (M1 and later): shut down, then press and hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears. Choose the USB stick and click Continue.

steps.t: Intel Mac: restart and hold the Option key until the drive icons appear. Click the USB stick.
steps.warn: Intel Macs with a T2 chip (2018 to 2020) refuse USB sticks until you allow it: start in Recovery (Command R), choose Utilities, Startup Security Utility, and tick "Allow booting from external or removable media".
ex: Icons appear for Macintosh HD and for the stick, often called EFI Boot or Install macOS. Click the stick, then the arrow under it.

sections.heading: If the stick is not in the list
steps: Try a different USB port, ideally one on the back of a desktop or directly on a laptop rather than through a hub.
Windows Fast Startup can make the key ignored: in Windows hold Shift while clicking Restart, then Use a device.

Some rescue sticks do not start with Secure Boot on. Enter the BIOS (usually F2 or Del at power on), find Secure Boot under Boot or Security, set it to Disabled, press F10 to save, and turn it back on afterwards.
Make sure the stick was written correctly: with Ventoy or Rufus, not by just copying the ISO file onto a plain stick.

title: Finding a computer's model, system and serial number
summary: Where to read the make, model, serial number and system version, which repair shops, warranty checks and downloads ask for.

sections.heading: The quick way: MendKit
steps: Open MendKit. The Dashboard shows the system version, processor and memory.
Click View all specs and temperatures for the full hardware list.
Open Reports. The top line shows the computer's maker, model and serial number.

sections.heading: Windows without MendKit

steps.t: Press the Windows key and R together, type winver and press Enter.
steps.see: A box saying Windows 11 or 10, the version (such as 24H2) and the build number.

steps: For model and serial, open Terminal and type: wmic bios get serialnumber, or look on the sticker underneath a laptop or on the back of a desktop.

steps.t: Click the Apple menu at the top left and choose About This Mac.
steps.see: The Mac's model and year, chip, memory, macOS version and serial number. Click the serial number to copy it.

steps.t: Open Terminal and type: hostnamectl
steps.see: The distribution and version, kernel, and on most computers the maker and model.

title: Back up before you fix anything
summary: The simplest safe way to copy someone's files before a repair, so nothing can be lost whatever happens.
need: An external drive or large USB stick

sections.heading: Why first
steps: Most repairs are safe. But a failing drive can stop working completely at any moment, and the stress of a scan or repair can be what finishes it.
A restore point protects Windows settings, not documents and photos. Only a copy on another drive does that.

sections.heading: How to do it with MendKit

steps.t: Plug in an external drive or USB stick with more free space than the person's files take.
steps.tip: Open MendKit's Dashboard: if any drive card does not say Healthy, back up before anything else and copy the most precious folders first.

steps.t: Open Migrate and click Back up to a drive.
steps.see: A list of the user accounts and folders: Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Music, Videos, Downloads and browser data, with sizes.

steps.t: Choose the external drive, tick what to copy and click Start.
steps.see: Progress in the bottom panel. Photos and videos can take an hour or more.

steps: When it finishes, open the drive in File Explorer or Finder and check that the folders are there and that a few photos and documents open.
Keep the drive somewhere safe until the repair is finished and the person has checked their files.

sections.heading: Without MendKit
steps: Windows: open File Explorer, select the folders in the user's folder and drag them to the external drive.
Mac: plug in a drive and let Time Machine use it, or drag the home folder's Documents, Desktop and Pictures to the drive.
Photos in the Photos app on a Mac live in one file, Photos Library, in the Pictures folder. Copy that whole file.

title: Windows Safe Mode and recovery
summary: How to reach Windows' own recovery menu and Safe Mode when Windows misbehaves or will not start.

sections.heading: Reach the recovery menu

steps.t: If Windows starts: click Start, then the power button, then hold Shift while clicking Restart.
steps.see: A blue screen titled Choose an option.

steps: If Windows will not start: switch the computer on and, as soon as the logo appears, hold the power button until it switches off. Do this three times. On the fourth start Windows opens Automatic Repair, then click Advanced options.

steps.t: Choose Troubleshoot, then Advanced options.
steps.see: Startup Repair, Startup Settings, Command Prompt, Uninstall Updates, System Restore and System Image Recovery.

sections.heading: What each option does
steps: Startup Repair: Windows tries to fix whatever stops it starting. Try this first.
System Restore: goes back to an earlier restore point, such as "MendKit before repair". Files are not touched.
Uninstall Updates: removes the most recent update, which helps when trouble started straight after one.
Startup Settings: restart into Safe Mode (press 4) or Safe Mode with Networking (press 5).
System Image Recovery: puts back a full backup image made in MendKit's Backup & Erase screen. It replaces everything on the drive.

sections.heading: Using Safe Mode
steps: Safe Mode starts Windows with only Microsoft's basic drivers. If the problem is gone in Safe Mode, a driver or program is the cause.
You can run MendKit in Safe Mode with Networking to scan for malware or remove a bad program.
Restart normally to leave Safe Mode.

steps.t: If the screen asks for a BitLocker recovery key, the drive is encrypted. The key is a 48-digit number.
steps.tip: Find it on another device at aka.ms/myrecoverykey, signed in with the person's Microsoft account.
steps.warn: Without the key the files cannot be read by anyone. Never reset or reinstall until you have it.

title: Staying safe: scams and fake support
summary: How to tell real help from a scam, and what MendKit will and will not do on a computer.

sections.heading: Signs of a scam

steps.t: A pop-up or phone call says the computer is infected and gives a number to call. Microsoft, Apple and banks never do this.
ex: "WARNING! Your computer has been locked due to suspicious activity. Call Microsoft Support at 1-8xx-xxx-xxxx immediately." This is always a scam, however official it looks.

steps: Someone asks you to install a program so they can "fix" the computer, then asks for payment, gift cards or your bank login.

A website says you must call or pay before it will let you leave. Close the browser: on Windows hold Ctrl and Shift and press Esc, select the browser and click End task. On a Mac press Command, Option and Esc.

sections.heading: What MendKit does and does not do
steps: MendKit only runs the commands in its own lists. It never asks for card or bank details and never sends your files anywhere.
Remote support (RustDesk) only starts when you click Open RustDesk and read out the code. Only do that with someone you contacted yourself.
Emailing a report opens a draft in your own mail program; nothing is sent until you press Send.

sections.heading: If you think you were scammed

steps.t: Disconnect the computer from the internet: unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi.
ex: Windows: click the Wi-Fi icon at the bottom right and turn Wi-Fi off. Mac: click the Wi-Fi icon at the top right and switch it off. Or unplug the network cable.

steps.t: In MendKit, run Check for remote access on the Dashboard and remove the programs the scammer installed.
steps.tip: See the guide "Remote access audit".

steps: From a different device, change your email and banking passwords.
Call your bank on the number on the back of your card if any money, card details or banking was involved.
Run "Pop-ups or strange behaviour" from the Dashboard for a malware scan.

title: Getting started with MendKit
summary: Your first run: what to do before you start, the two modes, and the safest order to work in.

sections.heading: Before you start
steps: Plug a laptop into power. Repairs, scans and transfers can take an hour or more, and a laptop that dies part-way through a repair can be left worse off.
Save any open work and close other programs, so their files are not locked while MendKit works.
If Windows says it is waiting to restart for an update, restart first. Repairs can stall while an update is half installed.

steps.t: Back up anything that cannot be lost.
steps.tip: See "Back up before you fix anything". MendKit saves a restore point before repairs, but that does not protect documents and photos.

sections.heading: Finding anything

steps.t: Type a word or a problem into the Search everything box at the top left, such as printer, pop-ups, slow, wifi or deleted photos. Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac) jumps to it.
steps.see: Results grouped as Fix a problem, Repair tools, How-to guides, Single repair steps, Settings you can undo, Free tools and Screens, best match first. Click Start or Open beside one.
steps.tip: Everyday words work: "pop-ups" also finds adware, browser and scam tools, and "printer won't print" finds the printer fixes. Results that need Technician mode switch it on for you.

steps: Press Escape or clear the box to go back.

steps.t: Open MendKit from the Start menu (Windows), Applications (Mac) or the applications menu (Linux).
steps.see: The first time, a Welcome screen lists the permissions MendKit needs. See "Permissions setup".

steps.t: Allow what is listed, then click Start using MendKit (or Skip for now).
steps.see: The Dashboard: the computer's name, system, processor, memory, free space and drive health.

steps.t: On Windows, click Restart as administrator on the Dashboard and click Yes.
steps.see: The badge at the bottom left turns green and says Administrator.
steps.tip: On a Mac or Linux there is nothing to restart: MendKit asks for your password when a step needs it.

sections.heading: Simple mode and Technician mode
steps: MendKit starts in Simple mode: Dashboard, Migrate, Updates, Hardware Tests, Crash Analyzer, ISO Library, Undo Center, How-To Guides, Reports and Permissions. Results are in plain language.
Tick Technician mode at the bottom left to add Repair, Tools, Tweaks, Setup Profiles and Backup & Erase, the live output panel, exit codes and the full logs.
Simple mode only runs safe recipes and will not carry on with a repair if a restore point cannot be saved. Leave it on for customers.

sections.heading: The safest order to work in
steps: Read the Dashboard cards. A drive that does not say Healthy needs its files copied off before anything else.
Run Health report under Other fixes. It changes nothing and tells you what is wrong.
Pick the problem under What is the problem?, or click Fix my computer for a general service.
Read the results, restart if asked, and check the problem is gone.

steps.t: If something got worse, use the Undo Center or System Restore.
steps.tip: See "Undo Center".

sections.heading: Finding your way around
steps: Every screen is in the menu on the left. The bottom panel shows what is running, a progress bar and Cancel.
The badges at the bottom left show administrator rights, "No internet" when the connection is down, and "Update available" when a new MendKit is out.
Every guide is in How-To Guides. Each tool on the Tools screen has a "How to use it" link to its own guide. Print this guide puts a guide on paper to follow at the bench.

sections.heading: Without internet
steps: MendKit checks the connection every minute and shows "No internet" at the bottom left when it is down.
Repairs, hardware tests, the crash analyzer, migration, tweaks, backup and erasing all work offline.
Tool installs, updates and ISO downloads need a connection, except tools saved for offline use (see "Offline installers"). Fix the network first with "No internet" on the Dashboard.

title: Permissions setup
summary: Giving MendKit the access it needs: Full Disk Access on a Mac, administrator rights on Windows, and camera and microphone for the hardware tests.

sections.heading: When it appears
steps: The first time MendKit opens after install, it starts on the Welcome screen. Open it again any time from Permissions in the menu.
Each permission shows a green tick when allowed, and amber or red when it is not. The screen checks again every few seconds, so you can switch things on in Settings and watch them turn green.
Items marked optional only matter for one feature, such as the camera test.

sections.heading: On a Mac: Full Disk Access

steps.t: Click Open Settings beside Full Disk Access.
steps.see: System Settings opens at Privacy & Security, Full Disk Access, and a Finder window shows MendKit in Applications.

steps.t: If MendKit is in the list, turn its switch on. If it is not, drag MendKit from the Finder window into the list, or click + under the list, choose Applications, MendKit and click Open.
steps.see: macOS asks for your password or Touch ID. Then MendKit's switch is on.

steps.t: If macOS offers Quit & Reopen, choose it. Otherwise click Restart MendKit at the bottom of the Permissions screen.
steps.see: Full Disk Access shows Allowed with a green tick.
steps.tip: Still Not allowed after an update of MendKit? Select MendKit in the Settings list, click −, then add it again. macOS keeps an old switch from the previous version that no longer applies.

sections.heading: On a Mac: camera, microphone and the rest

steps.t: Click Allow beside Camera.
steps.see: macOS asks "MendKit would like to access the camera". Click OK (or Allow).

steps: Do the same for Microphone.
Click Allow beside Control System Events and click OK when macOS asks. This lets MendKit list and remove login items.

steps.t: Click Send a test beside Notifications.
steps.see: A MendKit notification at the top right. If none appears, click Open Settings and turn on Allow notifications for MendKit.

steps: If something was refused before, Allow does nothing: macOS only asks once. Click Open Settings and turn MendKit on in that list instead.

sections.heading: On Windows
steps: Running as administrator: click Restart as administrator and click Yes.
Camera or Microphone shows Not allowed: click Open Settings. Turn on Camera access (or Microphone access) and further down "Let desktop apps access your camera" (or microphone).
Notifications: click Send a test. If nothing appears, Open Settings and turn notifications on.

sections.heading: On Linux
steps: Password prompt for repairs needs pkexec or sudo, which almost every desktop Linux has.
If the camera shows Not allowed, open Terminal, type sudo usermod -aG video $USER, then sign out and back in.

sections.heading: Finish
steps: Click Start using MendKit (or Done). Missing permissions are listed on the Dashboard on a Mac until they are given.

title: Dashboard and Fix my computer
summary: Reading the Dashboard, running a general service, fixing a specific problem, and asking whether a computer is worth fixing.

sections.heading: Read the cards
steps: Computer, System, Processor and Memory describe the machine.
System drive shows free space. Under 10% free turns amber: the computer will be slow and updates may fail. See "Free up space" (Mac) or run Low on space.
Each drive shows its health. Anything other than Healthy means copy the files off first.
Click View all specs and temperatures for every hardware detail and live temperatures (refreshed every 10 seconds).

steps.t: Click Fix my computer.
steps.see: A preview listing each step: restore point, drive check, system file repair, disk check, virus scan and cleanup, with how long each usually takes.

steps.t: Read the preview, choose what happens when it finishes (do nothing, restart or shut down), and click Start.
steps.tip: Allow 30 to 60 minutes. You can keep using the computer lightly, but do not start anything else in MendKit.

steps.t: When it finishes, read the results.
steps.tip: See "Reading the results".

sections.heading: What is the problem?

steps.t: Click the button that matches the trouble: slow, no internet, Wi-Fi dropping, pop-ups or strange behaviour, updates failing, crashing, printer, sound, Bluetooth, camera, and on a Mac also an app will not open, runs hot or shuts down, and out of space.
steps.tip: Hover over a button to see what it checks and how long it takes.

steps: Check the preview and click Start. MendKit runs the checks and fixes for that problem only.
Restart if the results ask you to, then test the problem again.

sections.heading: Other fixes
steps: Health report: checks everything and changes nothing. A good first run on any computer.
Network check: tests the connection step by step (adapter, router, internet, names) and measures download speed. It tests whichever connection is active, cable or Wi-Fi.
Network fix: resets the network settings. Needs a restart afterwards, and saved Wi-Fi networks may need their password again.
Backup checkup: says whether the computer has a working backup.
Check for remote access: looks for remote-control programs. See "Remote access audit".

sections.heading: Is this computer worth fixing?

steps.t: Click the button under Is this computer worth fixing?
steps.see: A verdict of keep, upgrade or replace, with the reasons: memory, drive type, age, battery, and Windows 11 readiness.

steps: It changes nothing. On Windows, run MendKit as administrator so the Windows 11 check can read the security chip.

sections.heading: Get help
steps: Click Get help on the Dashboard or on a results screen.
Email this report opens a draft in your mail program with what MendKit found. Read it, add a note and press Send yourself.

steps.t: Open RustDesk starts remote support. Read the ID and one-time password to your technician.
steps.warn: Only do this with a technician you contacted yourself, never with someone who called you.

title: Previews, running jobs and reading the results
summary: What the preview tells you, how to follow a job while it runs, and what each colour on the results screen means.

sections.heading: The preview
steps: Every recipe opens a preview first. It lists each step in order, what it does, how long it usually takes and whether it needs a restart.
Nothing has changed yet. Back leaves without running anything.
"Must succeed to continue" marks a safety step, such as saving a restore point. If it fails, the rest does not run.
On Windows, When it finishes lets you restart or shut down automatically. A restart or shutdown waits one minute and shows Cancel it.

sections.heading: While it runs
steps: The bottom panel shows "Running step 3 of 8", the step name, the time so far, the usual time and a progress bar.
You can use the computer lightly. MendKit runs one job at a time and tells you if you try to start another.
Cancel stops the current step. Steps already finished stay done.
If a step runs far past its usual time on Windows, it is usually waiting on Windows Update. Cancel, restart the computer and run it again.
When the window is behind others, a notification tells you the job finished.

sections.heading: Reading the results

steps.t: The headline says in one line whether all is well, something needs attention, or there is a problem.
ex: "All checks passed. Nothing needs attention."
"2 things need attention." followed by the list, amber first.

steps: Green tick: the check passed or the fix worked.
Blue "i": information only.
Amber "!": something to look at, such as updates waiting or a step that could not run.
Red cross: a problem MendKit could not fix. The text says what it means and what to do next.

steps.t: "Skipped, needs administrator": restart MendKit as administrator and run it again.
ex: Dashboard → Restart as administrator → click Yes in the Windows box → run the same recipe again.

steps: If the results say to restart, restart before deciding whether the fix worked.

sections.heading: Keeping and sharing results
steps: Save customer report (PDF) makes a one-page summary with a health score, what was found and fixed, and what to watch for. Save it or print it.
Copy report text copies the summary to paste into an email or a job ticket.
Every run is kept in Reports.

title: Repair: recipes and single commands
summary: Running a whole repair recipe or a single command yourself, in Technician mode.

sections.heading: Open it

steps.t: Tick Technician mode at the bottom left and click Repair.
steps.see: Recipes at the top, then every single command, each with how long it takes and tags for "admin" and "restart". On a Mac, a Mac tools section comes first.

steps: Type in the search box to find a recipe or command by name or by what it does.

sections.heading: Run a recipe

steps.t: Click Run beside the recipe.
steps.see: The preview of every step.

steps: Click Start.

steps.t: Read the results and restart if asked.
steps.tip: "Continue even if a restore point cannot be created" lets a technician go ahead when System Restore is turned off. Leave it unticked unless you have another backup.

sections.heading: Run a single command

steps.t: Click Run beside the command. It starts straight away, without a preview.
steps.warn: Commands tagged restart change things that only finish after a restart. Network reset commands drop the connection briefly.

steps: Watch the output in the bottom panel, then read the results.

sections.heading: Also on this screen
steps: Remote access audit: finds remote-control programs. See its guide.
Reinstall assistant: for when repairs do not hold. See its guide.
Mac tools (Mac only): Startup items, Free up space, Fix an app that will not open, and Check another drive. See "Mac tools".

title: Tools: installing and removing free tools
summary: Installing the trusted free tools MendKit knows about, checking which are installed, and removing them again.

sections.heading: How it works
steps: Each tool installs from its official source through the system's own package manager: winget on Windows, Homebrew on a Mac, and apt, dnf, pacman, zypper or Flatpak on Linux.
Only tools that work on this system are listed. The Licence column shows whether a tool is free for business use or for home use only.

sections.heading: Install tools

steps.t: Tick Technician mode and click Tools.
steps.see: Every tool with its job, licence, Status (Installed or not) and, on Windows, an Offline column.

steps.t: Tick the tools you want, or use Select all, then click Install selected.
steps.tip: Already-installed tools are skipped automatically.

steps: On Windows, run MendKit as administrator first so installs do not stop to ask. On a Mac or Linux, type your password when asked.

steps.t: Wait until each Status says Installed.
steps.tip: A Mac needs Homebrew for tool installs. If it is missing, MendKit says so and offers to install it.

sections.heading: Use and remove them
steps: Click How to use it beside any tool to open its guide.
To remove a tool, click Remove on its row, or open the Undo Center, which lists every tool MendKit installed.

sections.heading: If an install fails
steps: Check the internet connection (the No internet badge shows when it is down).
On Windows, if winget itself is missing or broken, run Updates first; winget comes with the App Installer from the Microsoft Store.
Open Reports and View log for the exact error.

title: Offline installers
summary: Saving tool installers while online, so they can be installed on a computer with no internet.

sections.heading: Save them while online
steps: In Technician mode open Tools. Tick the tools you will want offline.
Optional: click Check download sizes to see roughly how much space they need.

steps.t: Click Save selected for offline use.
steps.see: Each tool downloads into the cache. The Offline column then shows its version and size.
steps.tip: Save again later to pick up newer versions. Change folder moves the cache, for example to a USB stick.

sections.heading: Install without internet
steps: Run MendKit as administrator. Without internet there is nothing to ask permission part-way through.

steps.t: On the Tools screen tick the tools and click Install selected.
steps.see: The button reads Install from cache, and the saved copies are used automatically.

sections.heading: Carry them to other computers

steps.t: Build a technician USB stick in the ISO Library and tick Offline installers.
steps.tip: See "ISO Library and technician USB".

steps: A few tools run without installing; their saved copy opens straight from the cache. Microsoft Store apps cannot be saved.
On Linux (apt, dnf or pacman) each tool is saved with the packages it needs that this computer lacks, so install them on the same Linux version. Not available on a Mac yet.

title: Migrate: moving to a new computer over the network
summary: Copying files, settings and the list of apps from an old computer to a new one on the same network.
need: MendKit on both computers
Both computers on the same network
Both plugged into power

sections.heading: What moves and what does not
steps: Moves: Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Music, Videos, Downloads and other folders you choose, browser bookmarks, Firefox and Thunderbird profiles, LibreOffice and VS Code settings, and a list of installed apps.
Does not move: programs themselves (they are reinstalled from the list), and saved passwords (see "Moving saved passwords").
Works between any two of Windows, macOS and Linux. Folders land in the matching place.
Nothing on the new computer is overwritten. A different file with the same name is kept beside it as "name (migrated)".

steps.t: Install and open MendKit. Click Migrate, then Receive on this computer.
steps.see: A six-digit code in large numbers and "Waiting for the old computer".

steps.t: If Windows asks whether to allow MendKit on networks, tick Private networks and click Allow.
steps.warn: Both computers must be on the same network (the same Wi-Fi or router). Guest Wi-Fi often blocks this.

sections.heading: On the old computer

steps.t: Open MendKit, click Migrate, then Send from this computer.
steps.see: 1. What to move: each folder with its size. 2. The new computer: a list of computers found on the network.

steps: Tick what to move. Leave Downloads unticked if it is mostly old installers.

steps.t: Click the new computer in the list.
steps.tip: If it is not listed after a minute, check both are on the same network and that Receive is open on the new one.

steps.t: Type the six-digit code shown on the new computer and click Start.
steps.see: Progress on both computers. Large photo and video collections can take hours over Wi-Fi; a network cable is much faster.

sections.heading: Afterwards, on the new computer
steps: Read the results. They list what was copied and any files that could not be read.

steps.t: Click Reinstall apps from the old computer.
steps.see: The apps that could be matched are installed from official sources. Apps with no match are listed so you can install them yourself.

steps.t: Open each browser and check the bookmarks, then move the passwords.
steps.tip: See "Moving saved passwords".

steps: Keep the old computer untouched for a week or two, until the person is sure nothing is missing.

title: Backing up to a drive and restoring
summary: Copying files to an external drive, restoring them on any computer, and keeping a weekly backup.
need: An external drive with enough free space

steps.t: Plug in the external drive. Open Migrate and click Back up to a drive.
steps.see: 1. What to back up, with sizes. 2. Where to save it.

steps.t: Tick what to back up and click Choose drive or folder to pick the drive.
ex: Ticked: Documents (12 GB), Pictures (48 GB), Desktop (2 GB), Browser bookmarks
Drive: E: Backup Plus (2 TB, 1.6 TB free) → the backup goes in E:\MendKit Backup\ANN-LAPTOP 2026-11-18

steps.t: Click Start.
steps.see: A MendKit backup folder on the drive, with the files in plain folders you can also open yourself.

sections.heading: Restore on this or another computer

steps.t: Plug in the drive. Open Migrate and click Restore from a drive.
steps.see: A list of the backups found on the drive, newest first, with the computer name and date. Choose one and click Restore.

steps.t: Choose the backup folder on the drive, tick what to restore and click Start.
steps.see: Files arrive in the matching folders. Nothing already on the computer is overwritten.

steps: Click Reinstall apps from the old computer to install the apps from the saved list.

sections.heading: Weekly backup
steps: In Migrate, under Keep a regular backup, click Choose the backup drive and pick the external drive.

steps.t: Click Turn on the weekly backup.
steps.see: It runs every Friday at 12:30 and only copies new and changed files.

steps: It is silent when all is well. If the drive is not plugged in, MendKit shows a notice so it is not forgotten.
The button beside it opens the system's own backup (File History on Windows, Time Machine on a Mac) if you want both.

title: Copying files from an old drive
summary: Getting a person's files off a computer that will not start, by connecting its drive to a working computer.
need: A USB adapter or enclosure for the drive
A screwdriver for the old computer

sections.heading: Get the drive connected

steps.t: Take the drive out of the old computer.
steps.tip: Laptops: usually a few screws on the bottom. SSDs are small cards (M.2) or 2.5-inch boxes. Mac drives from 2016 on are soldered in and cannot be removed this way.

steps: Connect it to the working computer with a USB adapter, enclosure or dock that fits the drive type (SATA or NVMe).
On Windows, run MendKit as administrator, or the old user's folders cannot be read.

sections.heading: Copy the files
steps: Open Migrate and click Copy from an old drive, then Choose the old drive.

steps.t: Pick the drive itself, its Users (or home) folder, or one person's folder.
steps.see: 2. Whose files: the people found on the drive. 3. What to copy: their folders with sizes.

steps.t: Choose the person, tick the folders and click Start copying.
steps.tip: If the drive is failing (clicking noises, very slow, errors), copy the most important folder on its own first, such as Pictures.

steps: Read the results. Files that could not be read are listed.

sections.heading: If it does not work
steps: "No files could be read": run MendKit as administrator on Windows, and unlock BitLocker (Windows) or FileVault (Mac) drives first. BitLocker needs the recovery key from the owner's Microsoft account.

The drive does not appear at all: try another adapter or port. Check Disk Management (Windows) or Disk Utility (Mac). A drive that is not detected anywhere needs professional data recovery; do not keep trying, as that can make it worse.
Nothing on the old drive is changed, and saved passwords are not copied.

title: Moving saved passwords
summary: The safe way to move saved website passwords between browsers and computers.

sections.heading: Why MendKit does not copy them
steps: Browsers lock saved passwords with a key tied to the old computer, so copying the files does not work, and moving them as plain text is risky.
The safe way is each browser's own sync or export.

sections.heading: The easiest way: sign in to the browser

steps.t: Chrome or Edge: on the old computer sign in to the browser with the person's Google or Microsoft account and turn on sync. Sign in with the same account on the new computer.
ex: Chrome: click the round picture at the top right, Turn on sync, sign in with the Google account, then Yes, I'm in.
Edge: click the profile picture, Sign in to sync data, then check Settings, Profiles, Sync shows Passwords turned on.

steps: Firefox: sign in to a Firefox account on both. Safari: passwords sync through iCloud Keychain when both Macs or devices use the same Apple Account.

steps.t: Wait a few minutes, then open the password list on the new computer to check.
ex: Chrome: type chrome://password-manager/passwords in the address bar.
Edge: type edge://wallet/passwords.
Firefox: type about:logins.
The count should match the old computer, for example "142 passwords".

sections.heading: Moving them with a file
steps: In MendKit's Migrate screen, click Move saved passwords. It opens the right page in each browser found and explains each step.

steps.t: Export the passwords on the old computer, copy the file to the new one, and import it there.
steps.warn: The export file holds every password in plain text. Delete it from both computers and empty the Recycle Bin or Trash straight after importing. The exported file holds every password in plain text. Keep it on a USB stick, not the cloud, and delete it as soon as the import is done.
ex: Chrome: chrome://password-manager/settings → Export passwords → save as Chrome Passwords.csv
Then on the new computer: same page → Import passwords → choose the file.

title: Tweaks: changing settings safely
summary: Turning settings on and off with presets, and putting every change back exactly.

steps.t: Tick Technician mode and click Tweaks.
steps.see: Settings in groups (Privacy, Interface, Finder, Dock and others), each with a tick box showing whether it is on now, and presets at the top.

steps.t: Tick the settings you want on, or click a preset such as Standard or Minimal to tick a recommended set.
steps.tip: Read each description. Tweaks marked as needing a sign-out only show after signing out.

steps.t: Click Apply.
steps.see: Results listing each change.

sections.heading: Put things back
steps: Untick a tweak and click Apply to put that one back.
Undo all MendKit tweaks puts back every change MendKit made, using the exact values that were there before.
The Undo Center also lists each change with Put back.

sections.heading: Share a set
steps: Export ticked saves the ticked tweaks to a file. Import loads it on another computer. Setup Profiles can include tweaks too.

sections.heading: If a tweak will not change
steps: On Windows, run MendKit as administrator for tweaks that affect the whole computer. Some are locked by a work or school account.
On Linux, the tweaks shown depend on the desktop: GNOME, Cinnamon (Linux Mint), KDE Plasma or XFCE. Settings that do not exist on this computer are hidden.
On a Mac, a few need MendKit to have Full Disk Access (see "Permissions setup").

title: Updates, drivers and monthly maintenance
summary: Checking for and installing system and app updates, maker driver tools, scheduled maintenance and updating MendKit itself.

sections.heading: Choose which apps to update

steps.t: Click Updates in the menu on the left. In the App updates box, click Check for app updates.
steps.see: "Looking for updates" for up to a minute, then a table: each app with a tick box, its installed version and the new version in green. Nothing has changed yet.
ex: ☑ Mozilla Firefox   Mozilla.Firefox   131.0    132.0.1
☑ Notepad++   Notepad++.Notepad++   8.6.9    8.7
☐ Discord   Discord.Discord   1.0.9   1.0.9170   (only updates when chosen on its own)

steps.t: Untick any app you do not want updated now. Click a row anywhere to tick or untick it, or use Select all and Select none.
steps.tip: Leave an app on its current version when the person relies on it working exactly as it does, for example accounting software in the middle of tax season, or a program their work makes them keep on a set version.

steps.t: Click Update N selected (N is how many are ticked).
steps.see: The bottom panel updates each app in turn and the results list each one: updated, or the reason it could not be. One failure does not stop the others.
steps.tip: Close the apps first. An app that is open, such as a browser, often cannot be updated until it is closed.

steps.t: Click Check for app updates again to confirm the list is empty, or shows only the apps you left.
steps.see: "All your apps are up to date." when nothing is left.

steps: To update every app without choosing, click Update everything instead.

sections.heading: System updates

steps.t: Windows: click Open Windows Update and click Check for updates there.
steps.tip: Windows and driver updates come from Windows Update. Restart when it says "Restart required".

steps.t: Mac: in the macOS updates box, click Check, then Install updates.
steps.see: Apple's own updates, such as "macOS Sequoia 15.1.1". A restart is usually needed.

steps.t: Linux: in System updates, click Check, then Install updates.
steps.tip: Linux system updates install together: installing only some packages can leave the system broken, so there is no list to choose from.

steps: Restart if asked, then check again until nothing is left.

sections.heading: Drivers and firmware
steps: On Windows, the maker's own update tool (Dell, Lenovo, Intel) is offered when it fits this computer. See its guide.
Open optional driver updates goes to the Windows Update page listing maker drivers.
Back up drivers saves a copy of every third-party driver first, in case a new one misbehaves.
On Linux, the Firmware section uses fwupd.

sections.heading: Monthly light maintenance

steps.t: Turn on Monthly light maintenance. It runs on the 1st of each month at noon.
steps.tip: On Windows, turn it on while running as administrator so it can clean up and scan.

steps: It is silent. MendKit only opens and shows a notification when something needs attention.
Tick Also install app updates to include app updates. Run it now does it straight away.

sections.heading: Updating MendKit
steps: A few seconds after starting, MendKit checks for a newer version. "Update available" appears at the bottom left.
Open Updates. The MendKit itself card shows your version and the new one. Click Download the update, then Restart and install.
A portable or USB copy opens the download page instead. An update never installs while a job is running.

title: Hardware tests
summary: Proving each part works: keyboard, screen, speakers, microphone, camera, USB ports and the processor under load.

sections.heading: Before you start
steps: Open Hardware Tests and pick a test. Starting another test stops the one that was running.
Allow camera and microphone access when asked (see "Permissions setup").

steps.t: Click Keyboard and press every key once, including the function keys and the arrows.
steps.see: Each key turns green when pressed, and a count shows how many are left.
steps.tip: Keys that do nothing may be broken, or may be special keys the system handles itself (such as volume or Fn).

sections.heading: Screen

steps.t: Click Screen.
steps.see: The screen fills with one colour at a time.

steps: Look closely at each colour for dots that stay black, white or one colour (dead or stuck pixels), lines, or patches of different brightness.
Click to go to the next colour. Press Esc to stop.

steps.t: Click Left, then Right.
steps.see: A one-second tone from only that side. Sound from both, or none, points to a speaker or settings problem.
steps.tip: No sound at all: check the volume and output device, then run "No sound" on the Dashboard.

steps.t: Microphone: speak or tap near it.
steps.see: The level bar moves.

steps.t: Camera: the live picture appears.
steps.tip: A black picture with the light on usually means the privacy shutter is closed; a "no camera" message can mean a privacy switch or key is off.

sections.heading: USB ports

steps.t: Plug a USB stick or mouse into one port and click Refresh.
steps.see: The device is marked new, proving that port works.

steps: Unplug it, move to the next port and repeat.

sections.heading: Processor stress test
steps: Plug a laptop into power. On Windows, open LibreHardwareMonitor first so temperatures can be read.

steps.t: Choose a length and click Start.
steps.see: Every processor thread runs flat out. Fans get loud. Temperatures are recorded every five seconds.

steps.t: A healthy computer finishes without freezing or restarting and stays under about 90 °C.
steps.warn: If it switches off or freezes, stop: it is overheating or has a power or hardware fault. Clean the fans before trying again.

steps: The result is saved in Reports.

title: Crash Analyzer
summary: Finding out why a computer crashes, freezes or switches itself off, and what to do about it.

sections.heading: Run it
steps: On Windows, run MendKit as administrator so it can read crash dump files.

steps.t: Click Crash Analyzer.
steps.see: MendKit reads the last 30 days of crash records: blue screens, sudden shutdowns, hardware and drive errors, and apps that crashed or froze.

sections.heading: Read the result
steps: The headline names the most likely cause in plain words.
What was found lists each kind of crash, how often it happened and what it means. Blue screen stop codes are explained.
What to do, in order is the repair plan. Each step has a button that opens the right screen or starts the right repair. Work down the list.
Technician mode adds the raw detail (event IDs, stop codes, driver names) to each line of the timeline.

sections.heading: Tips
steps: Crashes that started after a new driver or update point at that driver: roll it back or update it from the maker.
Sudden shutdowns with no blue screen usually mean power or heat: check the charger, battery and fans.
Random crashes with different codes each time point at memory: test it with Memtest86+ from the ISO Library.

title: Setup Profiles
summary: Setting up a new computer in one run with a saved bundle of apps, tools and tweaks.

steps.t: Tick Technician mode and click Setup Profiles.
steps.see: The built-in profiles and any you have made, each listing its apps, tools and tweaks.

steps.t: Click Apply to this computer on the profile you want.
steps.see: MendKit installs the apps and tools and applies the tweaks, then shows one results screen.
steps.tip: On Windows, run as administrator first.

sections.heading: Make your own
steps: Click New profile, give it a name, and tick the apps, tools and tweaks.
Tick the apps installed on this computer copies the app list from the machine in front of you.
Built-in profiles cannot be changed; Copy and edit makes your own version.

sections.heading: Move profiles between computers
steps: Export saves a profile as a file. Import loads it on another computer.

title: Backup image and secure erase
summary: Making a full backup image before a risky repair, and erasing files or drives so they cannot be recovered.
need: An external drive for the image

sections.heading: Backup image before repair
steps: Tick Technician mode and open Backup & Erase.
Windows: connect an external drive formatted as NTFS with more free space than the Windows drive uses. Run MendKit as administrator.

steps.t: Choose the drive and click Create the backup image.
steps.see: Windows saves a WindowsImageBackup folder on that drive. Leave it where it is and do not rename it.
steps.tip: On a Mac this starts a Time Machine backup; on Linux it takes a Timeshift snapshot named MendKit before repair.

steps.t: To put it back: start Windows recovery (hold Shift and click Restart), then Troubleshoot, Advanced options, System Image Recovery.
steps.warn: Restoring an image replaces everything on the drive with the copy, including files made since.

steps.t: Under Secure erase, click to add files or folders to the list.
steps.tip: System folders and whole user folders are refused, to prevent accidents.

steps.t: Read the list twice. Type ERASE in the box and click Erase them.
steps.warn: Erasing cannot be undone. The files are overwritten with random data, then deleted.
ex: Type the word in capitals, exactly: ERASE. "erase" or "Erase" leaves the button greyed out on purpose.

sections.heading: Erase free space
steps: Overwrites the empty part of a drive so files deleted earlier cannot be recovered. Files still on the drive are not touched. It can take hours on a large drive.

sections.heading: Erase a whole drive

steps.t: For an external or second drive only: choose it, type ERASE and click Erase the drive. The drive the computer runs from is never offered.
ex: Erase choices look like: E: SanDisk Extreme (1 TB, USB)
The drive Windows runs from (C:) is never offered.

steps: To wipe the whole computer before selling it: on Windows use Reset this PC, Remove everything, Change settings, Clean data. On a Mac use Erase All Content and Settings. Or boot ShredOS from the ISO Library.
On SSDs and USB sticks, overwriting may not reach every old copy. Erase the whole drive, or use the maker's secure erase tool.

title: Reinstall assistant
summary: Reinstalling Windows over itself while keeping files, apps and settings, when repairs do not hold.

sections.heading: Before you start
steps: Back up the files anyway (see "Back up before you fix anything").

steps.t: Open Repair (Technician mode) and click Reinstall assistant.
steps.see: Before you start: checks for administrator rights, free space (at least 25 GB), power and BitLocker. Fix anything marked as a problem.

steps.t: Click the Option 1 button.
steps.see: Settings, System, Recovery opens.

steps.t: Click Reinstall now next to "Fix problems using Windows Update", and confirm.
steps.see: Windows downloads a fresh copy and reinstalls itself. Files, apps and settings stay. It takes an hour or more and restarts several times.

sections.heading: Windows 10, or when Option 1 fails: Option 2
steps: Click Get a Windows ISO and download the ISO that matches the installed edition and language.

steps.t: Under Option 2, click Choose the Windows ISO, pick the file, and click Start the repair install.
steps.see: Windows Setup opens.

steps.t: In Setup, choose "Keep personal files and apps" and follow the screens.
steps.warn: If "Keep personal files and apps" is greyed out, the ISO does not match the installed Windows. Stop and get the right edition and language, or files and apps will be removed.

sections.heading: Mac and Linux
steps: MendKit shows the steps for macOS Recovery (Reinstall macOS keeps files) and for Linux. See "macOS Recovery and First Aid".

title: ISO Library and technician USB
summary: Downloading rescue and installer images, and building a USB stick with portable MendKit, the images and offline installers.
need: A USB stick of 32 GB or more

sections.heading: Download images

steps.t: Click ISO Library.
steps.see: Installer and rescue images (Windows installers, Linux live systems, Memtest86+, Hiren's BootCD PE, Rescuezilla, GParted, ShredOS and others) with what each is for.

steps: Tick the ones you want and click the button to open each official download page. Download from there.

sections.heading: Build a technician USB

steps.t: In Technician mode, the Build a technician USB card is at the top of the ISO Library. Plug in a USB stick.
steps.tip: To start computers from the ISO files, install Ventoy on the stick first (see "Ventoy"). Ventoy erases the stick, so do that before copying.

steps: Click Choose the USB stick and pick it. Nothing already on it is removed.
Tick Portable MendKit, Offline installers (Windows) and the ISO files to copy. ISO files in Downloads are listed; Add ISO files adds others.

steps.t: Click Copy to the stick.
steps.see: Progress in the bottom panel. Copying again later only copies what changed.

sections.heading: Use it on another computer

steps.t: Open the MendKit folder on the stick and start "Start MendKit". Nothing is installed; settings, logs and undo records stay on the stick.
steps.tip: A portable copy runs on the same kind of system that made it: build it on Windows for Windows computers.

steps: To start a computer from one of the images, see "Starting a computer from a USB stick".

sections.heading: Which image for which job
steps: Windows will not start and you need files off it: Hiren's BootCD PE or a Linux live system.
Random crashes: Memtest86+, at least two full passes.
Clone a drive to a new SSD: Rescuezilla or Clonezilla.
Resize or repair partitions: GParted Live.
Malware that blocks scanners inside Windows: ESET SysRescue Live.
Wipe drives before selling: ShredOS.
Reinstall or repair-install Windows: the Windows 11 or 10 installer.

title: Undo Center
summary: Putting back settings MendKit changed, removing tools it installed, and restoring quarantined files.

sections.heading: What is listed
steps: Settings MendKit changed: every tweak, with when it was changed and Put back.
Tools MendKit installed: each with Remove.
Files set aside by MendKit (remote access audit, Browser cleanup, and startup items removed on a Mac): each with Put back.

steps.t: Click Undo Center and click Put back (or Remove) beside the item.
steps.see: A results screen confirming it.

sections.heading: Undoing a repair
steps: Repairs such as system file fixes cannot be reversed one by one.
On Windows, click Open System Restore and choose the restore point named "MendKit before repair". Files are not touched; programs and settings go back to that moment.

title: Reports and job history
summary: Finding past results, logs, the computer's serial number and a job history for your records.

sections.heading: Use it

steps.t: Click Reports.
steps.see: The computer's model and serial number at the top, then every job with when it ran and its result.

steps: Click View results to see a job's plain-language summary again, and save the customer PDF from there.
In Technician mode, View log shows the complete output, and Open logs folder opens the folder to copy logs from.
Export job history (CSV) saves the list of jobs, which opens in Excel or any spreadsheet.

title: Remote access audit
summary: Finding remote-control programs a scammer may have installed, and removing the ones nobody wants.

sections.heading: What it is for
steps: Scammers talk people into installing a remote-control program, then watch the screen or move money. The program often stays installed afterwards.
The same programs are used honestly by technicians, employers and family. Finding one does not prove a scam.

sections.heading: How to run it
steps: On Windows, restart MendKit as administrator first, so it can check every user's folders and remove what you choose.
Click Check for remote access on the Dashboard (or Remote access audit on the Repair screen).

steps.t: Click Scan this computer.
steps.see: After a few minutes, each remote-control program found, with where it was found and tags for "running now" and "starts with the computer".

steps.t: Ask the person about each one. Tick the ones nobody recognises or wants.
steps.tip: Keep anything their own technician, employer or family set up.

steps.t: Click Remove selected, read the confirmation and click Yes, remove them.
steps.see: Each program is closed, its service stopped and disabled, its uninstaller run, and loose copies moved to quarantine. An uninstaller window may ask you to confirm.

steps: Restart the computer and scan again to confirm they are gone.

sections.heading: Reading the results
steps: "Running now": active at this moment. "Starts with the computer": it comes back after every restart.
"Program file" lines are loose copies, usually in Downloads or on the Desktop, run without installing.
Quick Assist is part of Windows and listed for information only. It only connects when someone opens it and types a code.
The audit knows a fixed list of well-known products, so a clean result is not a guarantee.
Removal works on Windows and Linux. On a Mac it reports what it finds; remove those with Startup items and the app's own uninstaller.

sections.heading: After a scam
steps: See "Staying safe: scams and fake support" for what to do next: passwords from another device, calling the bank, and a malware scan.

title: Browser cleanup
summary: Removing unwanted extensions, notification pop-ups and settings forced into Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi or Firefox.

sections.heading: When to use it
steps: Pop-ups in the corner of the screen saying the computer is infected, even with the browser closed or on a different website. These are almost always a website that was allowed to show notifications.
The home page or search engine changed and keeps changing back.
A toolbar, coupon helper or "search assistant" nobody remembers installing.
The browser says "Managed by your organization" on a home computer.

sections.heading: Scan

steps.t: Close every browser window first.
steps.tip: Changes are only made while a browser is closed. Check the taskbar or Dock: the browser icon should not show a dot or line under it.

steps: Tick Technician mode at the bottom left, open Repair, and click Open beside Browser cleanup under Cleanup and recovery.

steps.t: Click Scan.
steps.see: A section for each browser profile on this account, with its extensions, the sites allowed to show notifications, and its home page, start-up pages and search engine if they were changed. If anything forces settings in from outside the browser, it is listed first under "Set from outside the browser".

steps.t: Extensions marked "not from the store" are ticked for you.
steps.tip: They were put there by another program rather than added from the Chrome Web Store, Edge Add-ons or Firefox Add-ons. That is how adware arrives.

steps.t: Read the rest. Untick anything the person uses, such as a password manager or an ad blocker they chose.
steps.tip: Not sure what one is? Search its name. A name you cannot find anything about is a good reason to remove it.

steps.t: Leave "Stop sites showing notifications" ticked.
steps.see: The list under it shows each site. Removing them all is safe: sites the person wants, such as email or chat, can ask again.

steps.t: Under "Set from outside the browser", tick the policies marked with things like "Sets the search engine" or "Forces extensions in".
steps.warn: On a computer from a workplace or school, these are put there on purpose. Leave them alone and ask their IT department.

steps.t: Click Clean selected.
steps.see: A result for each browser profile and each outside setting. Settings for every user need MendKit running as administrator (Windows) or your password (Mac and Linux).

sections.heading: If the home page or search engine is still wrong

steps.t: Beside the changed settings, click Open the reset page.
steps.see: The browser opens on its own reset page. If it opens on a normal page instead, type the address MendKit shows at the bottom of its window into the address bar.

steps.t: Click Reset settings (Firefox: Refresh Firefox).
steps.see: The home page, start-up pages and search engine go back to normal and extensions are turned off. Bookmarks, passwords and history stay.

sections.heading: If something comes back
steps: The browser is signed in with sync turned on and another computer still has the extension. Remove it on that computer too, or from the extensions page while signed in.
A program on the computer puts it back. Run Startup items and look for unfamiliar entries, and run the malware scan in Pop-ups or strange behaviour.
Scan again: a policy may have been added after the first scan.

sections.heading: Putting something back
steps: The old browser settings files and removed extension files are kept. Open Undo Center and click Put back beside the item, with the browser closed. On Windows, a removed policy is saved as a .reg file in the same folder; double-click it to put it back.

title: Recover deleted files
summary: Getting back deleted photos and documents: the quick places first, then a deep search of the drive or memory card.

sections.heading: Right away

steps.t: Stop using the drive the files were on.
steps.warn: Every file saved to it from now on can overwrite what you want back: downloads, installs, updates, even web browsing. For a memory card or USB drive, take it out and keep it aside.

steps: Have a second drive ready to save recovered files to, such as a USB drive with at least as much free space as the files you are looking for.

sections.heading: Look in the quick places

steps.t: Tick Technician mode at the bottom left, open Repair, and click Open beside Recover deleted files under Cleanup and recovery.
steps.see: Look here first lists the places on this computer where a deleted file may still be whole, with its name and folder.

steps: Recycle Bin or Trash: click the open button, find the file, then right-click it and choose Restore (Windows and Linux) or Put Back (Mac).

steps.t: Previous Versions (Windows): open the folder the file was in, right-click an empty part of the window, choose Properties, then the Previous Versions tab. Pick a date and click Open, then copy the file out.
steps.tip: MendKit shows how many saved copies there are when it runs as administrator. None saved means this will not help.

steps: File History (Windows), Time Machine (Mac) or Timeshift (Linux): plug the backup drive in, open it with the button, go back to a date when the file was there and restore it.
OneDrive, iCloud Drive or Google Drive: deleted files stay in the online recycle bin for about 30 days. Sign in on the website and look there.

sections.heading: Search the drive with PhotoRec

steps.t: If MendKit says PhotoRec is not installed, click Install PhotoRec.
steps.see: The bottom panel shows the install. It is free and open source, and is installed on this computer, not the drive being searched.

steps.t: Under 1, choose the drive the files were on.
steps.tip: A memory card or USB drive shows as removable. A drive marked "SSD inside the computer" gives a low chance: SSDs wipe deleted space within minutes.

steps.t: Under 2, tick the kinds of files to look for.
steps.tip: Photos and Documents are ticked to start with. Everything finds many more files and takes longer.

steps: Tick "Search the whole drive" only if the card or drive was formatted, or the computer says it needs formatting.

steps.t: Under 3, click Choose a folder and pick a folder on a different drive.
steps.warn: MendKit refuses a folder on the drive being searched, because saving there would overwrite the files being recovered.

steps.t: Click Start searching.
steps.see: On Windows, restart MendKit as administrator first. On a Mac or Linux, MendKit asks for your password. The bottom panel shows how many files have been found so far.
steps.tip: A memory card takes a few minutes; a large hard drive can take several hours. Cancel stops it, and files found up to then are kept.

steps.t: When it finishes, click Open the recovered files.
steps.see: A folder called "Recovered files" with the date, holding Photos, Documents, Videos, Music and Other folders.

sections.heading: Going through the results
steps: Recovered files have new names such as f0012345.jpg, and folders are not kept. Use the picture view in File Explorer or Finder to look through photos quickly.
Some files will be old, from long before, or only partly readable because part of them was overwritten. That is normal.
Copy the ones the person wants to keep to their usual folder, then the rest can be deleted.
On a Mac, the built-in drive is encrypted and clears deleted space, so only Time Machine or iCloud can bring files back from it. The search is for USB drives and memory cards.

sections.heading: When to stop
steps: If the drive clicks, is not seen at all, or the files are valuable and the search finds nothing, stop. A drive that is failing gets worse every time it runs. A professional data recovery service can often still help.

title: Phone photos and backups
summary: Copying photos and videos off an iPhone or Android phone with a USB cable, and checking iPhone and iPad backups on the computer.

sections.heading: Get the phone ready

steps.t: Plug the phone into the computer with its charging cable, and unlock it.
steps.tip: Some cheap cables only charge. If nothing happens, try the cable that came with the phone.

steps.t: iPhone or iPad: when it asks "Trust This Computer?", tap Trust and enter the passcode.
steps.tip: On Windows, Apple's free Devices app (or iTunes) may be needed once so Windows can see an iPhone. MendKit has a button to get it.

steps: Android: pull down from the top of the screen, tap the notification about USB, and choose File transfer (or Transfer files). On a Mac, choose Transfer photos (PTP) instead.
Keep the phone unlocked while copying. Turn screen lock off for a big copy, or tap the screen now and then.

sections.heading: Copy (Windows and Linux)

steps.t: Tick Technician mode, open Repair, and click Open beside Phone photos and backups under Cleanup and recovery. Click Look for phones.
steps.see: The phone, with how many photos and videos it holds and their size.
steps.tip: On Linux, open the phone once in the file manager first so the desktop connects to it.

steps: Choose the phone, then Choose a folder, such as Pictures or a USB drive.

steps.t: Click Copy new photos and videos.
steps.see: A folder named after the phone, with one folder per month (2026-07 and so on). The bottom panel shows the count as it goes; thousands of photos take a while.

steps.t: Click Open the folder and check some photos and videos open.
steps.tip: Nothing on the phone is changed or deleted. Run it again later and only new photos are copied.

sections.heading: Copy (Mac)

steps.t: Click Open Image Capture.
steps.see: Image Capture lists the phone on the left.

steps: Choose the phone, choose a folder in "Import To" at the bottom, and click Download All.
For an iPhone: to get the original photos rather than converted copies, set the iPhone's Settings, Photos, Transfer to Mac or PC, to Keep Originals.

sections.heading: Backups
steps: The screen lists the iPhone and iPad backups on this computer: which device, the iOS version, when it was last backed up, and whether it is encrypted.

A backup more than a month old is missing recent photos and messages. Make a fresh one before resetting or replacing the phone: on a Mac in Finder (choose the phone in the sidebar, Back Up Now), on Windows in Apple Devices or iTunes.
Encrypted backups also keep saved passwords, Wi-Fi and Health data, and need their password to restore. Write it down for the person.
Messages, WhatsApp chats and app data are not copied as photos are. They move with the phone's own transfer (Quick Start, Smart Switch) or its backup.

title: Windows tools
summary: The Windows tools on the Repair screen, step by step.

sections.heading: Before you start

steps.t: Restart MendKit as administrator (Dashboard, Restart as administrator, then Yes).
steps.tip: Without it, MendKit can only change items for your own account.

steps: Tick Technician mode at the bottom left, open Repair. Windows tools is the first section.

sections.heading: Startup items

steps.t: Click Open beside Startup items, then Scan.
steps.see: After up to a minute: programs that start when you sign in, scheduled tasks at sign-in or start-up, and background services, each with who made it and what it runs.

steps.t: Look for items marked "not signed", items marked "program missing" (leftovers), and names you do not recognise.
steps.tip: Items marked "hardware helper" belong to the sound, touchpad or graphics maker. Leave them on unless you know they are not needed. Items marked "part of Windows" cannot be ticked.

steps.t: Tick what to stop and click Turn off selected.
steps.see: Results for each item. Programs stay installed; services still start when a program needs them.

steps: Restart and check everything still works.
To undo, scan again and click Turn back on beside the item under Turned off. Items turned off here also show as Disabled in Task Manager's Startup apps, and can be turned on there too.

sections.heading: Free up space

steps.t: Click Open beside Free up space, then Measure.
steps.see: After a minute or two: free space, then each kind of clearable file with its size. The safe ones are ticked.
steps.tip: Close the browsers first if you want their caches cleared.

steps.t: Decide about the unticked ones.
steps.warn: Windows.old lets you undo the last Windows upgrade: once it is deleted you cannot go back. Crash dump files are what the Crash Analyzer reads, so run it first. Removing the hibernation file also turns off Fast Startup.

steps: Tick device backups only if the iPhone or iPad is backed up to iCloud or no longer used.

steps.t: Click Delete selected.
steps.see: Results for each item. Windows.old and upgrade leftovers open Windows' own Disk Cleanup progress window; let it finish.

steps: Large files and the Downloads folder are only listed. Click Show in folder and decide about them yourself.

title: Mac tools: startup items, space, damaged apps, other drives
summary: The four Mac tools on the Repair screen, step by step.

steps.t: Tick Technician mode, click Repair. Mac tools is the first section.
steps.tip: Give MendKit Full Disk Access first (see "Permissions setup"), or some folders cannot be checked.

sections.heading: Startup items

steps.t: Click Open beside Startup items, then Scan.
steps.see: Each program set to start with the Mac or run in the background, not made by Apple: who made (signed) it, what it runs, and whether it is running now. Login items are listed at the bottom.

steps.t: Look for items you do not recognise, items marked "not signed", and items marked "program missing" (leftovers from something already removed).
steps.tip: Search the item's name on the web if unsure. Names like com.google.keystone or com.microsoft.update belong to known apps.

steps.t: Tick the ones to remove and click Remove selected. Items for every account or the whole Mac need your password.
steps.see: They stop starting. Your own items can be put back from the Undo Center; system-wide items are moved to /Library/Application Support/MendKit/Quarantine.

steps: To remove a login item, click Remove beside it. The first time, click OK when macOS asks whether MendKit may control System Events.
Restart the Mac to make sure the items stay gone.

sections.heading: Free up space

steps.t: Click Open beside Free up space, then Measure.
steps.see: How much is free, then each kind of clearable file with its size: app caches, logs, iPhone and iPad update files, Mail attachments, Xcode files, the Trash, and each iPhone or iPad backup with its device name and date. Then files over 1 GB.

steps.t: The safe ones are ticked for you. Tick a device backup only if that device is backed up to iCloud or no longer used.
steps.warn: Deleted files do not go to the Trash. They are gone.

steps.t: Click Delete selected.
steps.see: Results with how much space was freed.

steps: For large files and Downloads, click Show in Finder and decide yourself. MendKit never deletes them.

sections.heading: Fix an app that will not open

steps.t: Use this when macOS says an app "is damaged and can't be opened", "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified", or "cannot be checked for malicious software".
steps.warn: Only for apps you trust, downloaded from the maker's own website. A real malware warning ("will damage your computer") must not be bypassed.

steps.t: Click Open beside Fix an app that will not open, then Choose the app and pick it in Applications.
steps.see: Whether it is blocked as downloaded from the internet, and whether its signature is valid.

steps: Leave "Also re-sign it on this Mac" ticked if the signature is not valid. Click Fix.
Open the app again. If macOS still asks, go to System Settings, Privacy & Security, scroll down and click Open Anyway.

sections.heading: Check another drive
steps: Plug in the external drive or USB stick. Click Open beside Check another drive.

steps.t: Choose the drive in the list. Click Check drive.
steps.see: "appears to be OK", or a list of problems.

steps.t: If problems were found, tick Repair problems it finds and click Repair drive. Type your password.
steps.tip: If repair fails, copy the files off the drive now: it may be failing.

title: Linux tools: startup items and free up space
summary: The Linux tools on the Repair screen, step by step.

sections.heading: Startup items

steps.t: Tick Technician mode, open Repair, and click Open beside Startup items, then Scan.
steps.see: Programs that start when you sign in and services that start with the computer. Ones the system needs are marked and cannot be ticked.

steps.t: Tick the ones you do not use and click Turn off selected. Services for the whole computer ask for your password.
steps.tip: Search a name you do not know before turning it off.

steps: Turned-off items are listed under Turned off by MendKit with Turn back on.
Restart and check everything still works.

sections.heading: Free up space

steps.t: Click Open beside Free up space, then Measure.
steps.see: Free space, then each kind of clearable file with its size. Safe ones are ticked.

steps.t: Tick what to delete and click Delete selected. Items for the whole computer ask for your password.
steps.warn: Deleted files do not go to the Trash.

steps: Large files are listed with Show in folder. Decide about them yourself.
